query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys intended for magnetic refrigeration, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles? Earlier work focused mainly on arc-melted ingots and melt-spun microribbons, where an ordered single-phase hexagonal state undergoes a first-order magnetostructural transition that produces a large but sharp and hysteretic entropy change; these bulk forms also have limited heat-exchange rates because of their low surface-to-volume ratio. Prior searches have largely emphasized composition-dependent changes in transition temperature or response amplitude, with most studies pursuing only one optimization variable. Under the constraints of avoiding rare-earth elements, retaining mechanical stability and low cost, enabling rapid heat exchange, and limiting hysteretic losses, specify one controlled intervention that would distinguish the proposed governing explanation from alternatives, the predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, the boundaries over which those predictions should hold, the prior observations that support the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Low-level Ag alloying in as-deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEAs improves the magnetic exchange homogeneity by promoting a more uniform chemical and microstructural ordering. This in turn broadens the magnetostructural transition and reduces hysteretic losses during low-field magnetic cooling cycles.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited single-phase hexagonal state that exhibits a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition with large, hysteretic magnetic entropy change and limited heat exchange rates.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled low atomic percent (e.g., 3–5%) Ag addition, substituting part of a magnetic element, during processing.
generation.conditions: Tests performed under low-applied-field (near ambient or room temperature) magnetic cooling cycles with identical processing parameters as the baseline. The intervention should be applied without altering the overall non-equiatomic balance to maintain mechanical stability and cost-effectiveness.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased homogeneity in local chemical order and microstructure (mediated by Ag) that tunes the distribution of magnetic exchange interactions.
generation.mechanism: Ag, as an FCC metal additive, plays a primarily structural role that reduces fluctuations in exchange energies among localized magnetic moments. This leads to a smoother magnetocaloric transition and lowers energy losses due to hysteresis by mitigating phase separation or abrupt structural changes during the magnetostructural transition.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-deposited baseline, the Ag-alloyed HEA will exhibit a broader temperature range over which the entropy change occurs, a reduction in hysteresis loss (i.e., a more reversible transition), and maintain a significant magnetocaloric response under low-applied-field conditions.
generation.baseline: The non-alloyed, as-deposited state shows a sharp, hysteretic, first-order magnetostructural transition with limited heat-transfer capabilities due to the low surface-to-volume ratio.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold for non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type HEAs processed under similar conditions (e.g., film deposition or rapid cooling routes) and near the transition temperature where magnetic cooling is applied. Extreme compositional variations or alternative processing that alters phase stability might fall outside this domain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal Ag content and its interplay with other alloying elements (like Pd, Ni, or Al) remain to be determined. There is uncertainty whether alternative FCC metal additives would yield similar effects under all processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of samples using the same non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy with identical processing conditions: one set as the baseline (no Ag addition) and one set with a controlled 3–5% Ag substitution. Subject both sets to low-applied-field magnetic cooling cycles while recording the magnetic entropy change, hysteresis loop area, and the width of the transition temperature range. Use X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy to assess microstructural homogeneity and chemical ordering.
measurements: Magnetic entropy change (ΔS) as a function of temperature
Hysteresis loop area from magnetization vs. magnetic field curves
Transition temperature width (ΔT) of the magnetostructural change
XRD patterns and microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM) for chemical ordering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ag-alloyed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant broadening of the transition temperature range accompanied by a reduction in hysteresis (i.e., similar or worsened hysteretic losses and entropy change profiles relative to the baseline), then the hypothesis that Ag addition improves magnetic exchange homogeneity and reduces hysteretic losses is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The unpredictability of geopolitical tensions and resulting supply chain and pricing instabilities make it imperative to explore rare earth free magnetic materials. As such, we have investigated fully transition metal based “high entropy alloys” in the context of the magnetocaloric effect. We find the NiFeCoCrPdx family exhibits a second order magnetic phase transition whose critical temperature is tunable from 100 K to well above room temperature. The system notably displays changes in the functionality of the magnetic entropy change depending on x, which leads to nearly 40% enhancement of the refrigerant capacity. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior provides direct evidence that heat treatment and Pd additions reduce the distribution of exchange energies in the system, leading to a more magnetically homogeneous alloy. The general implications of this work are that the parent NiFeCoCr compound can be tuned dramatically with FCC metal additives. The so-called “high entropy alloys” (HEAs) are a class of emergent transition metal alloys that hold great potential for advanced manufacturing, and which may impact magnetocalorics. These are near equimolar alloys with high entropy of mixing when in a random solid solution. These materials have been pursued for high hardness and resistance to wear and corrosion, which are attractive properties for a myriad of applications. Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx is an example HEA system with tunable magnetic properties. The addition of Pd was shown to change the critical temperature (Tc) from 300 to 500 K for x = 1 to 2, along with enhancement of the saturation magnetization; previous works have used high percentages of Pd as a stabilizing agent in similar high strength bulk alloys. In this work, we explore the magnetic properties of the Fe1Co1Ni1Cr1Pdx alloy family, as-rolled and after annealing, with low molar fractions of Pd. We find improvement in the magnetocaloric properties throughout the system. A detailed statistical analysis of the universal scaling behavior suggest this originates predominately from the homogenization of the alloy with both Pd and heat treatment.
